amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15, and a demonstrative pronoun standing in the phrase is itself what a written *this*, *that*, *these* or *those* renders; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentence has left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction.
amendments.why: NUM.11.3 and NUM.11.34 both had to be corrected inside the verse pass, and both for the same reason: the phrase shem hammaqom hahuʾ -> 'the name of that place' holds two article morphemes and a demonstrative pronoun, and the pass first read the single written the as fronted from the rectum's article. Rule 41 already yields the right answer, but only by combining two of its sentences that pull opposite ways. Its arthrous-chain sentence says the article takes the determiner standing before its own word and the construct takes the supplied the; its limit sentence says another morpheme licensing that determiner leaves the article unrepresented. Read in sequence, the second sentence looks as though it removes the phrase from the first, which invites exactly the fronting the two verses had to undo. The amendment names the demonstrative pronoun alongside the suffix and kol in the limit list, which the corpus supports (206 units align huʾ and its kin to a bare that, and 452 align an article to that where no pronoun competes), and adds the sentence that decides the case: a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the rectum's word, so nothing is fronted and the construct takes a supplied the. hammaqom hahuʾ, hayyom hahuʾ and haʿir hahiʾ recur throughout the Old Testament, so a later chapter meets this on its first page. I did not touch rule 29, whose fronting sentence is correct as written and is now cited by the qualification, and I promoted nothing about whether the agreement article fuses into the demonstrative's unit, because the corpus contains both treatments and a rule the corpus contradicts is worse than none; that choice is recorded as a chapter convention instead.

conventions: Demonstrative noun phrase (NUM.11.3, 11, 12, 13, 14, 32, 34). Where a noun carries its own article, its attributive demonstrative carries an agreement article, and the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase - kol ha-ʿam ha-zzeh -> 'all this people', ha-yyom ha-huʾ -> 'that day', ha-maqom ha-huʾ -> 'that place' - the demonstrative morpheme (zeh, huʾ) takes the written this or that and both articles are unrepresented, under rule 41's limit and rule 47's count. The chapter does not fuse the agreement article into the demonstrative's unit; the corpus holds a few such fusions (ha huʾ -> 'these' at 1KI.10.10, ha ʾelleh -> 'those'), and that reading remains the competing one, but rule 47 governs an agreement article the ASV leaves unwritten and this chapter follows it throughout.

hodesh yamim -> 'a whole month' (NUM.11.20, 11.21). The chain is rendered attributively under rule 28: yamim takes 'whole', hodesh takes 'month', and the supplied indefinite 'a' joins hodesh's unit under rule 15. No 'of' is placed, and the trailing yamim is not marked unrepresented.

report: Checked all 65 candidate lemma groups end to end, plus the 13 `added` units the table is blind to. Every multi-treatment bucket is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in different contexts, so no verse is patched.

The demonstrative noun phrase is the chapter's most repeated construction and is uniform across seven verses (3, 11, 12, 13, 14, 32, 34): the noun's article and the agreement article both go unrepresented and zeh / huʾ takes the single written this or that. NUM.11.3 and NUM.11.34 carry an in-verse correction of the construct-headed form shem hammaqom hahuʾ -> 'the name of that place', moving the written the off the rectum's article and onto the construct; both were corrected the same way, so nothing is left to reconcile between them.

Buckets that looked like splits and are not: ʾim opening a disjunctive question takes 'have' alone (11.12), 'or shall' (11.22) and 'or' alone (11.23), each read off the ASV; waw + loʾ is fused (11.19) only where one English word is written and split (11.15, 11.17, 11.25, 11.26) where two are; the suffix of bə-qirbo is unrepresented in 11.21 because it is resumptive under a written ʾasher and takes 'you' in 11.20 because it is not; lahem takes 'for' after 'be slain' and nothing after 'suffice' in both halves of 11.22; the second comparative kaph of 11.31 is unrepresented against one written 'about'. The nominal head choices (mixed multitude on multitude, young man on young, nursing father on nursing, chosen men on chosen) are one method - rule 31's subtraction test applied per lexeme - not two.

Supplied English is uniform: nine supplied object pronouns are added (11.1, 11.8 x4, 11.17 x2, 11.25, 11.31, 11.32), while every pronoun with an object morpheme to answer for it is aligned to that morpheme (11.8 s024, 11.12, 11.24, 11.28); the supplied 'but' of 11.20 and 'While' of 11.33 are added because no conjunction stands in either clause, whereas every subordinating that/to in 11.13, 11.16, 11.17, 11.21, 11.22 and 11.25 has a waw to carry it. Rule 29's count is followed in all sixteen construct chains that carry a written the.

BSB: 47 disagreements, none a genuine error. The recurring classes are the documented convention differences - object markers (rule 16), articles for which the ASV writes no the (rules 12, 29, 41), prepositions the ASV's recasting silences (rule 40), the lə of leʾmor (rule 27) and paragogic he and nun (rule 32). The named singletons are all resumptive or dropped elements the ASV renders once or not at all: nu in 11.6, huʾ in 11.7, ʿene in 11.10, hem in 11.16, zeh in 11.20, o in 11.21, ʾish in 11.25, ennu and the second bā in 11.33. No edge was changed to move the aggregate.

Two conventions recorded and one amendment to rule 41 returned; the amendment is what the two corrected place-name verses taught, and it settles the case for later chapters rather than leaving the over-broad fronting sentence in place.
